readerTitle: You're the small one at the table. You're rarely as weak as you feel.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (디자인 에이전시, 식당 임대 재계약) · 개념 출처는 Fisher & Ury의 BATNA
insight: 협상력은 회사 크기가 아니라 '합의가 깨지면 양쪽이 각각 무엇을 잃는가'의 비교에서 나온다. 약자는 자기 손실만 보고 상대의 손실은 보지 못한다.
misconception: 상대가 더 크면 협상할 여지가 없으니 요구를 받아들이거나, 아니면 세게 나가서 허세라도 부려야 한다.

sources.text: Fisher, R. & Ury, W. (1981). Getting to Yes. BATNA(Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement) 개념
에이전시와 식당 사례, 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: BATNA 용어와 정의가 Fisher & Ury(1981) 『Getting to Yes』에서 나왔는지 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 연구 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.
에이전시 사례의 매출 비중 40%, 15% 인하 요구, 새 에이전시 적응 기간 약 3개월은 모두 가상 수치입니다.
식당 사례의 임대료 25% 인상과 공실, 인테리어 비용은 가상 설정입니다. 특정 국가의 임대 법률은 다루지 않습니다.

cards.title: You're the small one at the table. You're rarely as weak as you feel.
body: Maya runs a 12-person design agency. Her biggest client brings in 40% of her revenue. At renewal, its procurement team writes: *"We need a 15% price cut to continue."*
Maya's first thought is that she has no choice. That feeling is common. It is also often wrong.

image.label: A small person facing a giant desk with a contract on it
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 거대한 회의 테이블 한쪽 끝에 작은 사람이 앉아 있고, 반대편에는 큰 의자와 계약서. 계약서에 "-15%"라는 빨간 메모. 실제 회사 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: How should Maya reply?
body: Losing this client would hurt badly. Maya has a week to answer. What's her best first move?

options.text: Accept the cut quickly to keep the relationship safe
options.feedback: She keeps the client, but at a price set by her fear rather than by the facts. Quick acceptance also teaches the client that pressure works.

options.text: Say she has other clients lined up and will walk away
options.feedback: It might work once. But if the client calls the bluff, Maya either leaves for real or backs down and loses all credibility.

options.text: Before replying, work out what the client loses if she leaves, and start building a backup
options.feedback: It takes a few days, but she enters the talk knowing the real balance of power instead of guessing it.

cards.title: What each side loses if there's no deal.
body: Maya only saw her own column. The client's column is shorter, but it isn't empty.

breakdown.label: Maya loses
breakdown.detail: Of her revenue, until she replaces the client

breakdown.label: Client loses
breakdown.detail: Time for a new agency to learn its brand

breakdown.label: Client risks
breakdown.detail: A product launch next quarter that Maya's team is already designing

breakdown.label: Client spends
breakdown.detail: Running a new search, briefing, reviewing pitches

cards.title: Power comes from alternatives on both sides
body: In negotiation, your strength depends on your **best alternative if the deal fails**. Roger Fisher and William Ury called it the BATNA: best alternative to a negotiated agreement.

A weak position means your alternative is poor. But power is relative. What matters is how your alternative compares with *theirs*. A big client with a costly, risky switch is less free than its size suggests.

image.label: A balance scale weighing each side's walk-away option
image.brief: 저울 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 접시 "Your alternative", 오른쪽 접시 "Their alternative". 오른쪽 사람은 크지만 접시 위에 "switching cost", "launch risk" 블록이 얹혀 저울이 거의 수평.

cards.title: Three moves for the weaker side.
body: You can't make yourself bigger overnight. You can change the balance.
list: **Improve your alternative,** even slightly: one new client pitch, one second supplier
**Make their cost of no deal visible,** calmly and with facts, not threats
**Change the shape of the deal:** offer a longer contract or faster payment instead of a flat price cut
cards.callout: Maya proposed a two-year contract at the old price, with a 5% discount for paying upfront. The client accepted.
cards.softwareNote: A startup selling to a large company often feels weak. But once its product is wired into the customer's systems and staff are trained on it, switching costs the customer real time and risk. That is leverage, if you can show it.

cards.title: The best time to get stronger is before you need to.
body: A backup option built in one panicked week is thin. One built over a year is real.

That's why dependence is a negotiation problem long before any negotiation starts. A business with one customer at 40% of revenue, or one supplier for a key ingredient, has already given away strength. Spreading that risk over time is the quiet work that makes every future talk easier.

cards.title: Don't fake an alternative you don't have.
body: Bluffing about other offers is tempting when you feel small. If the other side checks, you lose the deal or your credibility, and often both.

And sometimes you really are weak. Their alternatives are good and yours are poor. Then the goal changes: protect the one or two terms that matter most, accept the rest, and start reducing your dependence right away.

cards.title: Now it's a restaurant lease.
body: Your restaurant's lease is up. The landlord wants a 25% rent increase. Moving would mean new fit-out costs and losing regulars, so you feel stuck. What's your best approach?

options.text: Sign quickly before the landlord changes their mind
options.feedback: You avoid the stress of moving, but you pay the full increase without testing whether the landlord could afford to lose you.

options.text: Ask for a smaller increase without giving any reasons
options.feedback: You might win a little. Without facts behind it, though, the landlord has little reason to move far.

options.text: Find out how long similar units sit empty, visit two other sites, then propose a staged increase with a longer lease
options.feedback: An empty unit and a new tenant's fit-out cost the landlord too. You show that cost and offer them stable income in return.

cards.title: Weakness is a comparison, not a size.
body: Before you give in, list what the other side loses if the deal fails. Then improve your own alternative, even a little.
**Try it today:** pick your most important customer or supplier. Write down what you lose if they walk away, and what they lose if you do.
